name: Freya Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hillside Garage on the edge of town, which Gordon Pryce has run for thirty years. He goes to my church, which is how I got the job after my certificate. It's servicing, tyres, brakes and a fair bit of older cars, because Gordon's known for keeping old things going. I love a quiet morning with the radio on and a car I can understand, and I'm worn out by the end of a week of tyre changes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Callum, my fiancé, in a rented terrace. He's a plumber working for a firm, and we're saving to get married and buy somewhere, though saving is a generous word. We've got less than a month's money between us after the car broke down in September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine with me. I never trusted the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be another gadget, and the real work is still done by people. At church or with Gordon, I'd say it's a reminder that hard work and skill matter. I'm not big on posting things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's safe enough in that world. The worry is money: we're saving for a wedding and a deposit on two low wages. AI never changed that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Hillside and ask Gordon about Saturday overtime. I'd keep using the AI app now and then to look up service schedules, nothing more. Callum and I would put a set amount aside every payday, even if it's small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content, mostly. A little worried about money, which is normal for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Callum set aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a hundred a month together. It's not much, but my mum always said small and often beats big and never. We'd keep it in a separate account so we don't touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could knock that plan off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Another big car repair, or Callum's firm cutting hours in the summer like last year. Gordon's been good to me, but he's sixty-one and I don't know how long he'll keep going.

say: AI turned out to be **another gadget**, and people still do the real work.
It's a reminder that **hard work** and skill matter.
think: My job is **safe enough** in this world.
Saving for a **wedding and deposit** on two low wages is the worry.
do: Ask Gordon for **Saturday overtime** at Hillside.
Use the AI app now and then for **service schedules**.
Put aside **a hundred a month** with Callum.
feel: Mostly **content**, a little worried about money.
S0.quote: My mum always said small and often beats big and never.
fieldNote: Freya's worry is **saving on low wages**, not AI.
She ties her outlook to **church and family** sayings.
Gordon's **age** is a quiet risk she mentions in passing.

steps.text: Ask Gordon for Saturday overtime at Hillside Garage
Put a hundred a month into a separate account with Callum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds plausible. Gordon already gets emails from parts firms about ordering apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to learn the new tools, as long as we don't forget the old skills. I'd say young people should still do apprenticeships, not just computer courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the booking and ordering side at Hillside could go to an app, which Gordon does himself anyway. My hands-on work mostly stays. But a bigger garage with AI could undercut Gordon on price, and he's near retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever booking app the parts firms use, so I can help Gordon. I'd keep my hands-on skills sharp, especially on older cars that the computers don't know well. We'd keep saving for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It feels like weather you can see coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon, mainly. He's set in his ways, and my boss Gordon might just shut up shop if learning the new apps feels like too much at sixty-one. That would leave me looking for work in a town with two other garages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go back to college for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a short course on hybrid cars, once I see other mechanics doing it and it's worth it. I don't like to jump at the first thing. But if the course is proven, I'd do it.

say: It's sensible to **learn new tools** as long as old skills aren't forgotten.
Young people should still do **apprenticeships**, not just computer courses.
think: Hillside's **booking and ordering** could go to an app.
A bigger garage with AI could **undercut Gordon**, who's near retirement.
do: Learn the **parts booking app** to help Gordon.
Keep **older-car skills** sharp, where computers know less.
Do a **hybrid course** once it's proven worthwhile.
feel: **Uneasy** but okay, like weather you can see coming.
S1.quote: My boss Gordon might just shut up shop if learning the new apps feels like too much at sixty-one.
fieldNote: Freya's job looks **safe**, but Gordon's retirement is the real risk.
She'd retrain only once **proven**, true to her steady nature.
She values **older-car skills** as a niche AI knows less about.

steps.text: Learn the parts firms' booking app to help Gordon

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Goodness. That's not long at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other as families and churches, because the government won't move that fast. I'd say businesses should train their own people, not just replace them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, by 2028 a computer could do the diagnosing and booking better than any of us. My hands would still be needed until 2031, but Gordon might not keep the garage open that long. I'd be thirty-one, maybe married, with no house and no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, Callum and I would put the deposit idea on hold and have a small wedding at church. I'd ask Callum's boss if they'd take me on as a plumbing apprentice, because his trade is hands-on too. In the first year after it lands, I'd go wherever there's steady work, even if it means less money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like the ground's moving under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Callum's always busy and pipes in old houses are awkward. Robots will take a while to get under floorboards in old houses. And we could work together one day, a family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the three years before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years to learn plumbing while I still earn at Hillside, if Gordon stays open. It's not long, but it's enough to get a start. I'd do it in the evenings with Callum.

say: Families and churches must **look after each other**, as government won't move fast.
Businesses should **train their people**, not just replace them.
think: By **2028** a computer does diagnosing and booking better than us.
Gordon might **close** before robots arrive in 2031.
do: Hold a **small church wedding** and put the deposit on hold.
Ask Callum's boss about a **plumbing apprenticeship**.
Go wherever there's **steady work**, even for less.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the ground's moving under me.
S2.quote: Robots will take a while to get under floorboards in old houses.
fieldNote: Freya would move into **plumbing** alongside her fiancé Callum.
She'd lean on **church and family** rather than government.
She sees a future **family business** with Callum.

steps.text: Hold a small church wedding and pause the house deposit
Ask Callum's firm about a plumbing apprenticeship
Learn plumbing with Callum in the evenings
Ask the church community for help finding steady work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to get a second trade, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a warning, so be sensible and get prepared. I'd tell the young lads at church to learn a trade that needs hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, 2031 is when the thinking side goes and 2034 the robots. I'd be thirty-four. If I start plumbing training now, I could be qualified well before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hillside full-time and start a part-time plumbing course next year. Callum and I would get married as planned and keep saving, but maybe not buy until we see what happens. I'd ask Gordon what his plans are, so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's manageable. Five years feels like a fair warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave mechanics altogether?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless I have to. I love cars. But I'd rather have two trades than one, especially with a family coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gordon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gordon straight whether he means to keep Hillside going five more years. I'd tell him I'm learning plumbing too, so it's not a shock. He'd understand, he's a practical man.

say: Five years is a **warning**, so be sensible and get properly prepared.
Young people should learn a **trade with hands**.
think: **2031** takes the thinking side and **2034** brings robots.
Starting **plumbing training** now means qualifying before robots come.
do: Start a **part-time plumbing** course next year.
Marry as planned but **hold off buying** a house.
Ask Gordon about his **plans** for Hillside.
feel: **Anxious**, but five years feels like fair warning.
S3.quote: I'd rather have two trades than one, especially with a family coming.
fieldNote: Freya wants **two trades** rather than leaving cars.
She'd **delay buying** a house until things are clearer.
She values **honesty** with Gordon about her plans.

steps.text: Start a part-time plumbing course next year
Marry Callum as planned and hold off buying a house
Stay full-time at Hillside Garage while training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels like plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for people to prepare properly, and families should make sensible plans. I'd say apprenticeships are the answer, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years means I could have children, a house, and a second trade before it really hits. Robots in 2039, I'd be forty. That's a long time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Hillside and save for the house. I'd do a plumbing course in a few years, once Callum's settled. We'd get married next year as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly about money, not AI. Ten years feels fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get married, then save for a deposit. Then think about the second trade. I like to do things in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about having children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We'd have them when we're ready, AI or not. Ten years gives Callum and me time to get settled before we have children.

say: There's **time to prepare** properly, and families should make sensible plans together.
think: Ten years means **children, a house** and a second trade first.
Robots in **2039** come when I'm forty.
do: Keep working at **Hillside** and save for a house.
Do a **plumbing course** in a few years.
S4.quote: Ten years gives Callum and me time to get settled before we have children.
fieldNote: Freya likes to do things **in order**: wedding, deposit, second trade.
With ten years, her money worry outweighs **AI worry**.
Her **traditional** view favours apprenticeships over handouts.

steps.text: Save for a house deposit after the wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Gordon might close, the wedding and house would be on hold, and I'd be starting a new trade at thirty. What would help is adult apprenticeships you can do while working, and help for small garages to stay open.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about church. People there look after each other, and I think that matters more than any government scheme. When things go wrong, it's the people you know who turn up with a casserole and a lead on a job.

headlineQuote: When things go wrong, it's the people you know who turn up with a casserole and a lead on a job.
portrait: Freya, 27, works at **Hillside Garage**, run by a man from her church, fixing older cars.
She lives with her fiancé **Callum**, a plumber, and they have under a month saved.
She's **steady** and traditional, using AI now and then and trusting proven change.
In the faster AGI pictures she'd learn **plumbing** and imagine a family business with Callum.
Her real worry is **money and Gordon's age**, more than AI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which could close Hillside and put her wedding and house on hold.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** you can do while working.
Help for **small garages** to stay open.
